title: Comfortable While the Nation Crumbles
overview: Amos warns the wealthy, self-assured leaders of Israel and Judah that their luxury and pride will not protect them from the disaster that is coming.

parts.label: False security at the top (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Amos speaks to the leading men of Zion (Jerusalem, capital of Judah) and Samaria (capital of the northern kingdom of Israel), who felt safe because their nations seemed strong. He points to Kalneh, Hamath and Gath, powerful cities that had already fallen, and says that pushing the day of disaster out of mind only hurries it on.

parts.label: Feasting while ignoring the ruin (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: They lounge on couches inlaid with ivory, eat the best lamb and veal, play music, drink wine by the bowl and wear costly oils, yet do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph, meaning the northern kingdom, whose main tribes traced back to Joseph. Since they put themselves first, they will be first into exile, and their feasts will end.

parts.label: The LORD's oath (v. 8)
parts.note: The LORD swears by his own self, the strongest oath possible, that he hates Jacob's pride and its fortified palaces. He will hand over the city and everything in it, which likely means both Samaria and Jerusalem.

parts.label: Death in every house (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: Amos pictures houses great and small smashed, and one house where all ten people die and a relative must burn the bodies, something rare in Israel and perhaps due to plague. It is unclear who then warns against mentioning the LORD's name, or why: one old reading has the relative silencing a survivor about to thank God, while others hear fear of drawing more of God's attention.

parts.label: Justice turned to poison (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Horses on rocky cliffs and oxen plowing the sea are absurd, and so is a nation that turns justice into poison. The leaders boast of taking Lo Debar and Karnaim, names that sound like 'nothing' and 'horns' (a symbol of strength), but a nation, usually identified as Assyria, will crush them across the very borders they had just won.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter condemns wealth and comfort in themselves or mainly the indifference and injustice that came with them.
think: What makes it easy to stay comfortable and unbothered while people nearby are struggling?
